client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away last year from cancer. I keep trying to push through at work, but I'll just be sitting at my desk and suddenly I can't concentrate on anything — it's like my mind just goes blank or I start thinking about her and lose track of everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because nothing is going to bring her back, so I don't really know what I'm doing here.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom, and then trying to hold yourself together at work while grief keeps pulling you back to her. I can hear in the way you're speaking, soft and fast, almost like you're holding something fragile, that this pain is real and present even as you push forward. You're right that nothing will bring her back, and I'd never suggest otherwise — but what we can work on together is helping you find a way to carry this grief without it swallowing you whole, so those moments at your desk feel a little less like you're disappearing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you're not trying to give me some silver lining or tell me it'll all be okay, because I've heard that enough and it just feels hollow. But I'm not sure what "carrying it without it swallowing me" even looks like — like, when I'm at my desk and it hits me, I don't feel like I have any control over it at all. It just happens, and then I feel guilty for not being able to focus, like I'm failing at the one thing I'm supposed to be holding together right now.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — feeling like you're failing because grief interrupts your focus — is actually a thought worth gently questioning, because your mind isn't malfunctioning when it drifts to your mom, it's doing exactly what a mind does when it loves someone it's lost. I notice there's a real tension in how you're speaking, like you're moving quickly through something that feels urgent and painful at the same time, and I want you to know that losing concentration at your desk isn't a character flaw — it's a sign of how significant this loss is. What if we started there — not by trying to stop the grief from coming, but by loosening the grip of that guilt that piles on top of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but it's hard because my boss has already noticed I've been off, and I got a pretty pointed comment last week about missing a deadline. So it doesn't really feel like just a thought I can reframe — there are actual consequences happening, and that makes the guilt feel pretty justified, not like something I'm just making up. I guess I'm skeptical that telling myself "it's okay to grieve" is going to change the fact that I'm falling behind.
therapist: You're absolutely right that the consequences are real — a missed deadline and a boss who's noticed isn't just a thought, and I don't want to minimize that. But I'm hearing something in your voice right now — there's an urgency and intensity there, almost like you're bracing for more to go wrong — and I wonder if the pressure you're putting on yourself to perform as if nothing happened might actually be making it harder to focus, not easier. What if the goal isn't "it's okay to grieve" as a permission slip, but rather figuring out some concrete, small strategies to help you function at work *while* grieving — not instead of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Okay, that framing actually makes a little more sense to me than just being told to be gentler with myself, so I'm willing to hear what those strategies might look like. But I guess my worry is that anything we come up with is going to feel manageable in here and then completely fall apart the moment I'm actually sitting at my desk and it hits me out of nowhere. It's like there's no warning, it just comes, and I don't know how you plan for something like that.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a kind of urgency — tells me this worry isn't abstract, it feels very alive and immediate, like you're almost anticipating the next time it hits you even as we sit here. That's actually really useful information, because you just proved that the grief *does* give you a signal — right now, your body and voice are ramping up just thinking about it, and that activation itself can become something you learn to notice as an early cue. What we can work on is building a very small, simple "anchor" response for exactly that moment at your desk — not to stop the grief, but to give you something concrete to do in the ten seconds after it arrives, so you're not just at its mercy.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess I never thought about it as a signal before, I always just experienced it as something that ambushed me with no warning. But I'm a little skeptical about the "ten seconds" thing — like, when I'm in it, ten seconds feels like nothing, and I'm not sure I'd even remember to do whatever the anchor is supposed to be, because my brain kind of goes offline. What would this even look like in practice?
therapist: Your skepticism is fair, and I notice even as you're asking this your voice has a kind of high, quick energy to it — like your mind is already stress-testing the idea before we've even built it, which actually makes sense given how ambushing this has felt. The anchor doesn't need to be something you *remember* so much as something you *practice* until it becomes almost automatic — something as simple as putting both feet flat on the floor and taking one slow breath, which works precisely because it bypasses the part of your brain that's gone offline and speaks directly to your body. We'd practice it here, repeatedly, so that when the wave hits at your desk, your hands and feet remember what to do even when your mind can't.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually sounds simpler than I expected, which I appreciate, but I guess my hesitation is that it feels almost too small for how big the feeling is — like, my mom died, and I'm supposed to press my feet into the floor and breathe? Part of me worries that doing something that small is going to feel dismissive of how much I actually miss her, like I'm just trying to shut the feeling down instead of actually feeling it.
therapist: That concern tells me something really important about you — you don't want to manage your grief away, you want to honor your mom, and that's not a problem to fix, that's love. I notice you're speaking softly but quickly, like this worry is delicate and real at the same time, and I want to be clear: the breath and the feet aren't there to shut the feeling down or tell it to leave, they're there to help you stay upright *while* you feel it, so the grief moves through you at your desk instead of taking you completely under. The goal was never to make missing her smaller — it was to make you just sturdy enough to hold it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: When you put it that way — "sturdy enough to hold it" — something about that actually landed differently than anything else you've said today, because it doesn't feel like I'm being asked to move on or get over it. I think I've been so afraid that coping means betraying her somehow, like if I stop falling apart I'm admitting she didn't matter that much. I'm still not sure I fully believe the feet-and-breathing thing will work, but I think I'm at least willing to try it without feeling like I'm doing something wrong.
therapist: What you just named — that fear that coping means betraying her — is one of the most painful and most common things grief does to people who loved deeply, and the fact that you can see it so clearly right now feels like a real moment of insight. I can hear in your voice something that sounds like cautious relief, like a door cracking open just slightly, and I want to honor that without pushing too hard on it. Trying the anchor without feeling like you're doing something wrong *is* the first step — and every time you use it, you're not moving away from her, you're learning to carry her with you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That phrase "carry her with you" is doing something to me right now that I wasn't expecting, because it reframes the whole thing in a way that doesn't feel like loss has to mean absence. I think I've been operating under this idea that grief is something I need to get through and come out the other side of, and the possibility that she could just stay with me while I also function — I don't know, that feels both comforting and really sad at the same time. I'm not sure I'm ready to fully sit with that yet, but I don't think I want to leave it behind either.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — your voice high and fast, like something is moving through you faster than you can quite catch it — tells me this realization is landing somewhere deep and real, not just as an idea but as something felt. That mix of comfort and sadness you're describing isn't a contradiction, it's actually what love looks like when it outlives someone, and you don't have to resolve it or be ready for it today. It's enough that you're willing to hold it here, and we can come back to it as many times as you need to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think I needed someone to tell me that it doesn't have to be resolved, because I've been putting so much pressure on myself to figure out what grief is supposed to look like and when I'm supposed to be done with it. There's a part of me that's still a little guarded about all of this, like I'm waiting for the session to end and then reality to hit again when I'm back at my desk tomorrow morning. But I think today gave me something small to hold onto, and maybe that's enough for now.
therapist: The guardedness you're naming is honest and wise — there *will* be a moment tomorrow at your desk, and I don't want to oversell what one session can do. But I notice something in your voice right now, high and quick, like you're both moved and bracing at the same time, and I think that tension itself is worth trusting — it means you're taking this seriously rather than just feeling better in the room and forgetting it by morning. "Something small to hold onto" is not a consolation prize; for someone carrying what you're carrying, it's exactly the right place to start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what's sticking with me most is that you didn't try to talk me out of the guardedness, because usually when I admit I'm skeptical about something people try harder to convince me, and that just makes me pull back more. I'm going to try the feet and breathing thing tomorrow, but I want to be honest that if it doesn't work I might come back here feeling like I was right to be skeptical in the first place. I guess I just wanted to say that out loud so it doesn't feel like a secret I'm keeping.
therapist: Saying that out loud instead of keeping it as a secret is itself a kind of courage, and I want you to know that if you come back tomorrow having tried it and feeling like it didn't work, that's not a failure — that's just more information we work with together. I can hear in your voice something that sounds almost like cautious openness, high and quick, like you're taking a small risk by being this honest, and I don't take that lightly. Your skepticism has a seat at the table here — it always did.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
